newsitem.title: MALI: Upcountry clashes, opposition boycott mar Mali poll.
newsitem.headline: Upcountry clashes, opposition boycott mar Mali poll.

text.p: Upcountry clashes and an opposition boycott disrupted Sunday's rerun parliamentary election in Mali, one of the stars of Africa's 1990s democracy movement. Witnesses said the turnout appeared low.

The capital, Bamako, was calm, with police and paramilitary gendarmes out in force. But state radio and witnesses reported polling stations and cars being ransacked and torched in strongholds of the radical opposition outside the capital.
The election is part of only the second set of multi-party polls in the arid and impoverished nation, which was widely praised for a successful transition to multi-party democracy in 1992.
The radio and witnesses spoke of trouble in San and Segou, east of Bamako, Kolokani to the north, and Sikasso to the southeast.
An unconfirmed report spoke of at least one death in San. Residents said polling was suspended briefly there.
The constitutional court had scrapped the original parliamentary election on April 13, citing chaos and irregularities.

The opposition wanted the whole election timetable revised but President Alpha Oumar Konare, a historian elected in 1992, pressed ahead with a presidential election on May 11 with only minor modifications. He won a new five-year term, but the main opposition also boycotted that election.
Turnout on April 13 was around 30 percent. On May 11, when Konare was re-elected, it was just 28 percent.
Almost 600 candidates from Konare's Alliance for Democracy in Mali (ADEMA), 18 other parties and 13 independent lists wre contesting the 147 seats in the national assembly.
Just over five million Malians were eligible to vote in the election, which is being run by an independent commission.
On Saturday, members of the radical opposition ransacked and torched ADEMA's national headquarters and a town hall in Bamako after a protest march by 3,000 militants.
Konare played down the pre-poll violence. "Violence from whatever quarter can never resolve problems," he said after voting.
His prime minister, Ibrahim Keita, said those responsible for the vandalism would be prosecuted.
Konare himself said Sunday's polling would enable the mainly Moslem former French colony "to consolidate the rule of law and deepen the democratic process".
Mali received fulsome praise for its 1992 transition from Moussa Traore's dictatorship to a multi-party system.
It won independence from France in 1960 and takes its name from a pre-colonial African empire that built its power on gold and flourished when Europe was in the Middle Ages.
Gold remains a major source of foreign exchange, with Mali on course to become Africa's third largest producer.

The 18-party radical opposition alliance includes supporters of Moussa Traore, who remains in detention, and of independence leader Modibo Keita, who ruled Mali as a pro-Soviet one-party socialist state.
First results were expected on Sunday night. Final results, to be ratified by the constitutional court, were likely within 72 hours. The poll will run to a second round on August 3.
